RECONSTRUCTED TEXT — Open Library search-inside, 2026-09-06
===========================================================

THIS FILE IS NOT A SCAN AND NOT A TRANSCRIPTION FROM A READ COPY. Both books below are
lending-restricted on the Internet Archive and neither has been read. Every line of quoted text
here was assembled by walking overlapping phrase queries against
https://openlibrary.org/search/inside.json, which returns a highlighted window of roughly twelve
words around each match. Searching the last four words of one window returns the next. The
contract for that endpoint is recorded at f_4933.

WHAT IS RECOVERED: two passages, both continuous within themselves, both walked to their own
sentence boundaries. WHAT IS NOT: everything else in either book. Page images for both are
blocked (see the ACCESS FAILURE note at the end), so nothing here has been checked against the
page. The OCR's own line-break hyphens ("real- ized", "Mon- treal") are left in place because
they are evidence of where the scan broke, not of how the book reads.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ITEM 1. Dictionary of Literary Biography, Volume 362: CANADIAN LITERARY HUMORISTS
        (Detroit: Gale Cengage Learning, 2011). ISBN 9780787681807.
        "A Bruccoli Clark Layman book."
        Internet Archive: canadianliterary0362unse — scan leaf 456
        The entry is "Stuart McLean (1948– ) / David C. Greer", per the volume's own
        contents list in the Internet Archive metadata.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

RECOVERED PASSAGE (continuous, walked in both directions from the Kanawana hit):

    "... novelist Mordecai Richler's creative- writing class. During the summer vacation of 1969
    he got a job as a counselor at Kamp Kanawana, near Saint-Sauveur, Quebec, about an hour from
    Mon- treal. By the summer of 1971, the year he graduated from the university with a bachelor
    of applied social science degree, he was a section director at the camp, and he was an
    assistant director during the summers of 1974 and 1975. In an unpublished 19 May 2010
    interview he discussed the significance of this experience: "for the first time in my life,
    I real- ized I had found a place where I could be good at something . . . or as good as
    everyone else anyway .. . a place where I could fit in and be competent and contribute to the
    greater good. Which is a very important thing for a young person's growth and development."
    McLean recorded a Vinyl Cafe radio show at the camp in July 2005. After graduating ..."

The walk stops at "After graduating", which begins the next subject.

WHAT THIS ADDS, AND WHAT IT ONLY CORROBORATES. This project already holds McLean's 1969 start,
his section directorship in 1971 and his assistant directorship in 1974 and 1975 — the last two
from the camp's own directors' reports for 1974 and 1975, which are better sources than this
one. What is new is (a) the MONTH of the 2005 recording, July, where the article had only the
year; (b) a fuller version of the "contribute to the greater good" line, which this project held
only in the one-sentence form a CBC Montreal Radio Noon interview produced; and (c) the
existence of an UNPUBLISHED 19 MAY 2010 INTERVIEW with McLean, conducted for this volume and
therefore presumably held by its author, David C. Greer. That interview is a live archival lead
and is registered as such.

A CAUTION ON THE QUOTATION. The ellipses are the book's, not this project's; the internal
spacing (". . ." then ".. .") is the OCR's and should not be reproduced as printed. Because the
page image cannot be fetched, the quotation is given here exactly as the search index returns it
and is quoted in the wiki with its OCR artefacts silently normalised and that normalisation
declared.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ITEM 2. Armand B. Ball (1930– ), BASIC CAMP MANAGEMENT: AN INTRODUCTION TO CAMP
        ADMINISTRATION (Monterey, CA: Healthy Learning, 2012). ISBN 9781606792087.
        "An American Camp Association book."
        Internet Archive: basiccampmanagem0000ball_r5m1 — scan leaf 436
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

RECOVERED PASSAGE (continuous):

    "... Keewaydin Foundation. In Canada, the first organizational camp and first independent
    camp were both organized in the same year: 1894—YMCA Kamp Kanawana in Quebec and Camp
    Keewaydin (formerly Kamp Kah Kiou) in Ontario. All of these camps were exclusively for boys.
    In 1876 ..."

The walk stops in both directions at a subject change: "Keewaydin Foundation" ends the preceding
sentence, and "In 1876" begins a new one.

QUERIES RUN, in order:
  "1894—YMCA Kamp Kanawana in Quebec and Camp Keewaydin"
  "Camp Keewaydin (formerly Kamp Kah Kiou)"
  "were organized in the same year: 1894"        — 0 hits (the sentence does not read that way)
  "in Ontario. All of these camps"
  "organized in the same year: 1894"
  "and first independent camp were both organized"
  "the first organizational camp and first independent"

WHY IT MATTERS. This is the American Camp Association's own introductory textbook — the book a
North American camp administrator is handed — and it names Kamp Kanawana as CANADA'S FIRST
ORGANIZATIONAL CAMP, dated 1894. This project holds the 1894 founding well from the camp's and
the association's own records; what it did not hold was a statement of primacy from outside the
YMCA of Montreal, in a professional reference work, in print. It bears directly on the question
the Canadian Camping Association put to its own membership in 1969 — "we need to know who opened
the first camp in Canada" — and on the four competing long-continuity claims among Canadian YMCA
camps already recorded in this KB.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE. Ball is tertiary, gives no source, and is writing a textbook chapter,
not adjudicating a claim. "Organizational camp" is a term of art in the American camping
literature (a camp run by an organisation — a Y, a church, a agency — as against an independent
or private camp), so the sentence is a statement about two CATEGORIES, and it does not say
Kanawana was the first camp of any kind in Canada. Note also that it places Keewaydin in
Ontario, which is its Temagami operation; Keewaydin's own founding claim is 1893, in Maine.
Ball's date for Keewaydin therefore disagrees with Keewaydin's, and a source that is a year out
on one half of a sentence is not a source to lean on for the other half. Recorded as what a 2012
professional textbook says, not as a finding about 1894.

ACCESS FAILURE — page images, both items
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
https://archive.org/download/canadiankeybusin1999unse/page/n1148_w1600.jpg
  -> HTTP 403, 4,868 bytes of HTML, WITH the item's own details page sent as Referer.
The same endpoint serves images for unrestricted items (the Referer trap that returns a 43-byte
transparent GIF under HTTP 200 is a DIFFERENT failure and is not what happened here). A 403 with
an HTML body is the lending restriction. The same is expected of the two items above and was not
separately retried.

ROUTES NOT TRIED for either book: an Internet Archive borrow with an authenticated account;
Google Books snippet view; HathiTrust full-text search; a library copy. Gale's own Literature
Resource Center carries the DLB text and is the obvious route to Item 1 for anyone with a
university or public-library subscription — the McGill, Concordia and BAnQ subscriptions are all
plausible and none has been tried from here.
